newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Baht seen strong on trade-weighted basis - StanChart.
newsitem.headline: Baht seen strong on trade-weighted basis - StanChart.

text.p: The Thai baht, the victim of repeated speculative attacks following bearish foreign sentiment for the country's economy, remains in fact a strong currency, Standard Chartered Bank (StanChart) said on Tuesday.

While the baht has weakened by seven percent against the U.S. dollar since 1995, it has appreciated by 39 percent against the yen and 12 percent versus the mark since mid-1995, Stanchart said in a research bulletin.
The baht's slide against the dollar was an outcome of it being pegged to a basket of currencies in which the U.S. unit constituted an 80-85 percent weight.

"Given this basket, if the U.S. dollar appreciates by 50 percent against the yen, then mathematically the baht should depreciate by about one-eighth of 50 percent, which brings us to the 6-7 percent against the U.S. dollar," it said.
Stanchart said the negative sentiment plaguing the baht would automatically begin to dissipate once the dollar reversed its upward trend against the yen in the next six months.
Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan's recent comments about re-examining the baht basket once the currency has stabilised also pointed to a possible change in the baht's position against the dollar.

"If there is any change in the baht basket, then the most likely shift will be to reduce the U.S. dollar weight, and increase the weight of the yen and other Asian currencies because it better reflects the composition of trading partners," Stanchart said.

Stanchart sees a slim chance of a baht devaluation as such a move would damage investor confidence, hurt banks and finance companies in terms of their dollar loans and compromise the central bank's effectiveness.
It said the Bank of Thailand had sizeable foreign reserves to intervene in forex markets and if this failed, it could rely upon its Southeast Asian counterparts to provide support.
